newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - LIFFE fills market niche with new Euromark.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - LIFFE fills market niche with new Euromark.

text.p: LIFFE's one-month Euromark interest rate future will supply short-term hedging needs and boost its drive to be the dominant exchange after European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), analysts said on Monday.
Earlier, the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange said it would issue the contract on November 21 as part of the exchange's EMU strategy.
"This contract will be used increasingly in the countdown to EMU," said Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Capital Markets in London.
"Given the degree of EMU optimism, it couldn't have been launched at a better time," he said.

LIFFE said it had decided to start the contract after seeing a high level of liquidity in the over-the-counter (OTC) market, where people can trade the equivalent of one-month Euromark futures using the Forward Rate Agreement market.
"Liquidity has increased dramatically OTC," said a spokeswoman for LIFFE. "We felt that introducing the one-month Euromark contract would fit the needs of the market."
Traders said the number of customer requests for short term hedging instrument had recently increased. Using three-month futures to hedge one-month exposure was not specific enough, traders said.
"The more LIFFE can tailor-make its products to the market, the more interest it will get," said Robert Eller, a senior broker at Citifutures in London.
This will be particularly important as LIFFE vies for post-EMU business with the MATIF exchange in Paris and the DTB exchange in Frankfurt, analysts said.
He said the success of the contract would largely depend on LIFFE's marketing, particularly since many companies still view derivatives as a dirty word.
"Many companies are now over-careful after Leeson," he said, referring to Barings' trader Nick Leeson, who ran up $1.4 billion of losses in unauthorised derivatives trading.

LIFFE also said increased issuance of short term paper by the Bundesbank had inspired the move, and the exchange was keen to press its advantage in mark denominated contracts, which it believes will form the core for trade post-EMU.
"This will strengthen our position," the spokeswoman said. "We are already dominant in mark contracts and we are offering the market more alternatives."
The LIFFE spokeswoman said the exchange was still looking at whether the contract would need market-makers and would decide before the launch.
Roberts said initially the contract was likely to be attractive for speculators, while large hedge funds would wait on the sidelines until it found its feet.

"Later on it will start attracting U.S. mutual funds and European hedge funds who want to increase their efficiency in hedging short-term views," he said. "But it will start out as a pioneering thing."
